title: Notes of Ministry - 79 - June 1979

paragraphs.text: Jude is diverted from his original intention in writing this letter (Jude 3), but what has impressed me is that while he is diverted at first, he finally returns to the main line, and finishes with the main line. It is to be noted how often he uses the word ‘beloved’, showing a link with John who in a similar way feels the conditions described in the Revelation. Jude returns to what you might call the main line, that is, the primary thoughts of God—God’s love, eternal life, and the service of God.

So these ‘buts’ Jude uses are very encouraging, and in spite of the intrusion of contrary elements, which are not difficult to identify, he says, “But ye, beloved, remember the words spoken before by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ”, and then, “But ye, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, awaiting the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life”. While we are bound soberly to consider such contrary elements that we can readily identify (often within ourselves) that cause concern to us, and to others generally in the testimony, yet Jude returns to these ‘buts’—“But ye, beloved ...”.

Then in verse 20 he seeks to engage us with the greatest thoughts, and we are not only to be occupied with these things but we are to contend for them, as he says, “contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints”. I think that would apply to ourselves particularly now as to what through grace has been recovered to us. (?) The enemy is seeking constantly to undermine the truth that has come to us through beloved servants in the ‘recovery’, “the faith once delivered to the saints”; contend earnestly for that.

There will always be contention for the truth. The enemy will always seek to weaken it in us individually, or collectively, or universally; he will not give up. So the Revelation shows us in detail how these constant attacks are met.

But what one is concerned to encourage us with is Jude’s saying “But ye, beloved, building yourselves up”; that is what we can do. We are not to be unbalanced and over-occupied with the contentions, but we are to be on this positive line of building. David was on the conflict line, and we need that line, but Solomon was on the building line, and we can do this ourselves. “But ye, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, awaiting the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life”.

The Holy Spirit is always ready to help us to keep ourselves in the love of God. Keep yourselves in that area; it is always open to us. No matter what the contention might be, no matter what the pressure might be, no matter what the testings might be, we can always retreat, retire, so to speak, into this impregnable area—“the love of God”—and keep ourselves in it. Someone said, ‘Well, have you been in it today?’ How much have you thought about it today? How much have we kept ourselves in it? “Keep yourselves in the love of God, awaiting the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life”. There are no ‘ifs’ about that!

Then Jude finishes with this fine doxology. What a wonderful thing! The letter is written to meet these frightful incursions of evil and ends with this doxology, you might say a special one, an incomparable one in one sense. We sang about exultation, which encouraged me to read this—“To him that is able to keep you without stumbling, and to set you with exultation blameless before his glory, to the only God our Saviour, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, might, and authority, from before the whole age, and now, and to all the ages. Amen”. What an area that covers, “from before the whole age, and now”. It is not to be deferred or postponed, it is now; it is what we can continue with now, in the very presence of these opposing elements that the enemy would constantly seek to keep alive and seek to distract us with.

If there is a diversion, as you call them in this country, (we call them ‘detours’, which I suppose is French, but anyway it is a diversion) it gets you off the main route. The important thing is to get back on the main line and stay on it. It may seem a contradiction, but we sometimes have to divert. These matters of conflict have to be faced soberly, but we are assured of divine help in doing it. In the meantime let us not become preoccupied with them but take account of these ‘beloveds’. “But ye, beloved, building yourselves up”—that is what we can do ourselves “on your most holy faith”—that would include what we are to contend for, “the faith once delivered to the saints”. “Your most holy faith” involves keeping it in separation from evil. It is christianity held in a right way, a priestly way. Then, “praying in the Holy Spirit”—what resources we have! Then, “keep yourselves in the love of God”. May we continue, beloved brethren, in power in the service of God in this way. Solomon was engaged with building; he built the house and installed the ark and arranged the courses for the service, all on this positive line.

“But to him that is able to keep you without stumbling”—what material, what substance there is for us in these last two verses to enrich us for the service of God! We are to be set with exultation before His glory—our exultation—but I think it includes God’s exultation. In spite of the incursion of evil, in spite of the conflict, God is going to have the last word, and not only the last word, but with exultation. That is what you get in Revelation 19: 7—“Rejoice and exult”. “To him that is able to … set you with exultation blameless before his glory, to the only God our Saviour, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, might, and authority, from before the whole age, and now, and to all the ages. Amen”. What a triumphant note on which to finish a letter of this kind, certainly a corrective letter, but finishing with this note of exultation which would greatly enrich the service of God.

But what I would specially leave with us is to keep ourselves in the love of God. “But ye, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God”, as if while that is always available to us, it is not automatic, and we are responsible to keep ourselves in it. I am sure that is the way that the victory will be maintained and the service continued in power, linking with the primary thoughts of God and going right through to the end “from before the whole age, and now, and to all the ages.
Amen”.

Beloved brethren, we live in days of great gravity and the course of the testimony has always called for much sobriety and a continual sense of responsibility for all who partake of the Lord’s supper, and what I want to speak about now, as having the Lord to help us, is positive activities, positive actions. The Lord would help us as to the positive outlook of our spirits as well. It is a very important matter in these days that our spirits might be maintained at the right level. Among the unclean animals in Leviticus 11 is the groaning lizard, and the spiritual meaning of that would be to instruct us to keep our spirits rightly; to correlate the activities of our hands in serving in the assembly with a spirit which conduces in itself to the furtherance and the development of the work of God. It is a very important matter, beloved brethren, because as to fact we sometimes influence more by our spirits than we do by our actions. It is one of the very attractive things about the spiritual order of things. In man’s world a man’s measure is related to his activities, his achievements; they point to his accomplishments in a material sense; but the beauty of Christianity is what can be effected by persons in their spirits, as being marked by what is right.
I turned to this passage in 1 Chronicles 15 because in a sense it is historical in its bearing. A brother made reference in the reading to the

characteristics of a certain period, and what we would have to say humbly is that the ark was not carried according to the due order; we would all subscribe to that; that was what characterized that period, and humility has marked the dear brethren in regard to it, and I believe it does still. But in the recovery which marked David in this passage there comes to light something that did not so strongly characterize the time of failure, and that was the bringing in of this feature of song. What marked the original bringing up of the ark was the predominance of what was military; the writer in 2 Samuel 6: 1 perhaps enlarges upon that more than the writer in Chronicles. Of course, the analogy to history is clear; but when the recovery comes in in David, he moves again in the furtherance of his desire that the ark should find a resting place in Jerusalem and “spoke to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brethren, the singers, with instruments of music, lutes, and harps, and cymbals, that they should sound aloud, lifting up the voice with joy”. Without being imaginative, perhaps someone would have said to David, ‘Well, David, are you right; do you not think we should proceed into this matter with the utmost gravity, clothed in sackcloth, with your head bowed?’ But no; he gave instruction about this wonderful addition of bringing in the musical instruments and the singers, and I think that, beloved brethren, is an allusion to the spirit in which we should move in a conscious sense that the Lord has recovered a situation in His own grace, characterized by the spirit of joy and thanksgiving.

The passage in Colossians is the New Testament analogy to this—“Let the word of the Christ dwell in you richly”. What was the danger in Colosse? The allowance of the human mind and intellect, philosophy and vain deceit—intruding into the christian circle and causing Paul to be apprehensive

lest anyone would lead them astray. It was in effect a new cart, and therefore he brings forward in the Colossian epistle the glory of the Person of Christ, the ark in all its greatness and glory; he brings it forward, again assuring the saints that the great point of recovery was what was in mind. So Paul says, “Let the word of the Christ dwell in you richly”. I do not think there will be room for anything that is subversive if the word of the Christ is dwelling in us richly. It is a very remarkable expression, it seems to involve all that is connected with the glory of that Person. His greatness, and what He is in God’s thoughts as the centre of that vast universe of bliss; and we are to be occupied with it. “Let the word of the Christ dwell in you richly”—we are to be occupied with it, to be filled with it, to find it our constant theme of conversation. Then, “in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another, in psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to God”. That is the spirit of recovery; that is the spirit in which David took up the ark again to Jerusalem with these singers with the cymbals and with the lutes. You can almost read into this “psalms, hymns, spiritual songs”, these holy activities.

So, beloved brethren, what can we say about psalms? It is well taught amongst us that the psalms relate to experience. I do not think that they exactly refer to experience in conflict, that you can detail your part in the various crises, that you can give an historical account of things. I do not think that is a psalm. I think a psalm is an experience with divine Persons.

You can relate for the help and the encouragement of God’s people some experience of the help of divine Persons, where the Spirit has helped you in a testing exercise. He helped you as to how to deal with it.

and the spirit in which to deal with it. He helped you, and you could write a psalm about that, a spiritual song, an ascription to divine Persons, in other words, a heart welling forth so that God Himself gets a portion from every exercise in spiritual songs. Well, we want to be humble and yet we want to ponder in our spirits the greatness and the glory of Christ—and what has been brought back to us in this day of recovery despite what had come in in the new cart and the failure associated with it. In the recovery the Lord is giving us in ministry touches of freshness and power which are an evident testimony to the continuing presence of the Spirit amongst us.

If we turn again to 1 Chronicles 15 there are one or two beautiful touches. It says at the end of verse 20, “with lutes on Alamoth”; the note says, Probably ‘voices of young women’. That is fine! Are we not thankful to have our young people with us today? We must be thankful, leaving out the literal side of it, for the freshness of affection that the Lord is bringing out amongst His people. Then it says, “with harps on the Sheminith”, and the note reads, ‘eighth, probably the bass octave’. It would have reference to the depth of things; pure and holy depth of feeling enters into our spirits so that we are not trivial, we are not light; and then it says in verse 22, “And Chenaniah, chief of the Levites for the music” or, as the note says, ‘transport’.
Beloved brethren, we have been transported as coming to the gathering of the saints and had our spirits uplifted, getting a touch from a divine Person.

So in Colossians 3 we have, “whatever ye may do in word or in deed, do all things in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father by him”. What a spirit! What a spirit in which to move in and out amongst the brethren. Visiting an old sister,
you do it in the name of the Lord Jesus; it is the spirit in which you care for the Lord’s interests, “in the name of the Lord Jesus”.

One other point in this section is that as well as singers there are doorkeepers. Well, beloved, I would say you want to enlist the service of the doorkeeper in anything that is going to be done in this spirit. If you see any root of bitterness or malice or any sense of a grudge in regard to the past history of things, you need the doorkeepers so that your spirit is not damaged. That is why the doorkeepers come into it. We should be continually on the alert, so that our spirit is not affected or damaged by matters either universally or locally.

In 2 Chronicles 5, which is quite a remarkable passage, there is the synchronizing of the one hundred and twenty priests sounding the trumpets, and the singers, as mentioned in verse 13—“it came to pass when the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one voice to be heard in praising and thanking Jehovah”. It is a synchronizing, beloved brethren, of our spirits with the attestation of divine glory and supremacy in the assembly. These trumpeters!

O, beloved, what a sphere the assembly is! You have the constant attestation in the assembly as to the supremacy of divine Persons, as to the Lord’s supremacy, and as to the Father’s supremacy. I have said it once or twice recently, because it causes me a lot of concern, that there is nothing that tests me more if I hear it in the meeting than the expression as to the importance of giving the Lord the first place. It is one of the most common expressions amongst us, and yet if you ponder the implications of that statement, giving the Lord the first place, it involves every matter that comes up domestically, every matter that comes up in your local meeting, every matter that comes up circumstantially. I think it is one of the biggest tests that the Spirit can apply to an exercised believer—how we give the Lord the first place.

Here are these one hundred and twenty trumpeters, typically sounding the attestation of the supremacy of God consequent upon the installation of Christ in the point of highest glory, and every knee is going to bow to Him in that place. It says the singers and the trumpeters were as one. It is a matter in which your spirit is in perfect accord with the divine supremacy.

And then, when they were as one, they praised Jehovah for His loving-kindness, and it was then that “the house, the house of Jehovah, was filled with a cloud, and the priests could not stand to do their service because of the cloud; for the glory of Jehovah had filled the house”.

It is a wonderful psalm this—Psalm 136 would be in mind, “For he is good, for his loving-kindness endureth for ever”. Could you sing that in Redbridge? Could you sing that in London? Could we sing it in Edinburgh? “For he is good, for his loving-kindness endureth for ever”. Some authorities on the Old Testament Scriptures tell us that when David established the twenty-four courses, on festival occasions all were employed and twelve of the courses sounded the praise and the other twelve answered in the refrain. Think what that would be when twelve of the courses sang, “Give thanks unto Jehovah for he is good”, and the other half answered, ‘Yes, for His loving-kindness endureth for ever’. O, beloved brethren, the importance of unity in the truth, based on the supremacy of God being acknowledged, and our spirits being entirely in accord with it; it leads to the greatest triumph that can possibly be envisaged in the praise of God. There is nothing to equal it in its blessedness.
So it says in Ephesians 5, “And be not drunk

with wine, in which is debauchery; but be filled with the Spirit”. O, beloved brethren, be filled with the Spirit! Then there could be no question as to your spirit; there could not be any question as to the character of your spirit if you are filled with the Spirit. Our hearts would be always rejoicing, completely in accord with God’s great thoughts. “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and chanting with your heart to the Lord”; beloved brethren, how much of this is with us? How much in a practical sense are our spirits affected so that we are constantly expressing ourselves in this wonderful activity and in this wonderful service? Think of the edifying effect of this holy occupation. It is like Psalm 45, our hearts welling forth with a good matter. Perhaps we dwell too much on the past; perhaps we dwell too much on the current activities of persons who have departed from the truth.
There is a basis for consideration as to these better things.

We can never have too much of these psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, ‘giving thanks at all times for all things to Him who is God and Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, submitting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ’. You attest the supremacy of God; the trumpeters give expression to it; they attest the supremacy of God, the supremacy of the Lord. But it goes beyond that. This is the test—“submitting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ”. If the weight of that got into our spirits how meekly we would accept adjustment. I think that if our spirits are right, beloved brethren, we will get the answer; if our spirit is right we will get the answer to all that the Lord is saying in the assembly amongst His own, and contribute to the edifying, the building up and strengthening of God’s people in a positive way. That should be our heart’s desire and our life work.
May the Lord bless the word for His name’s sake.

There is an expression that at one time was used a good deal among the brethren; personally I have not heard it used very much in these days although that may not be so up here; the expression is ‘soul history with God’. Our fathers and forefathers were very fond of it as bringing before us the need for personal soul history with God. I have no doubt that studying the Scriptures and the ministry all enters into this soul history because the Scriptures are the word of God. The good teaching is the ministry of the Spirit to help us in the understanding of Scripture, to help us to grow in the knowledge of God. But I think soul history with God means more than that, valuable as that is. It would mean among other things that you turn every experience in life into a spiritual one because you take it up with God and thereby you learn to know God and to trust Him. How often I find I am deficient; something happens and I find that I do not trust God as I ought to trust Him; my confidence is lacking. Nevertheless God goes on with us as He did with Jacob so that in all the experiences of life, the ups and downs, as we say, of life, we should as turning them into spiritual experiences grow in and by the true knowledge of God. I wonder if we are doing so.

Now there is not in one sense such a call for dependence today as there was in early days, because in God’s mercy (and we receive it from Him) we have plenty to eat and drink, we have a good many things to help us and occupy us, and the many things which are mercies can make us independent of God; that is a tendency. If you receive a mercy from God, Satan will immediately use that, if he can, to turn you away from God. God would have us to take all these things up with Him, so that whatever our circumstances in life, whether we are well off or poor (and our Lord said you will have the poor always with you) we should be using all those circumstances and turning them all, in God’s ways, into spiritual experiences.

I would like to ask, is each of us here developing soul history with God? Some of us are a little older, some are young, some very young, but this is a personal matter. I could have referred to others who suddenly appear on the page of Scripture; Elijah suddenly appears; you say, ‘That was very sudden that God took him up’. I do not think so. I would say that behind his sudden appearing was a wealth of spiritual experience with God. He says, “the God ...

before whom I stand” (1 Kings 17: 1), as though it was characteristic of him to stand before God. He appears abruptly and has an abrupt message, he suffers with the people, but I believe behind that there was soul experience. Now I would like to encourage every one of us to develop this. It is not outdated, it is something that each of us needs if we are in God’s testimony. It is very easy to become acquainted with the terms of spiritual things, especially when you are continually listening to them, but you might well be acquainted with the terms of spiritual things without having the experience of the things themselves. So I would exhort each of us to go to God; if
ministry does anything it sends us to the Lord for ourselves, that is the intention. If not, it could be what men call just brain-washing.

I was speaking to a man at the office the other day about the Lord and he said, ‘Well, yes, but what I am afraid of is being brain-washed. I do not think like you think, and I do not belong to the people you belong to; I do not keep their company, and I do not want you to brain-wash me, that is what I am afraid of. I am not saying that what you are saying is wrong’. I could only reply, ‘Well, it is simple enough for you to go to the Lord for yourself. You have a Bible, read it and go to the Lord for yourself, do not just listen to what I say. See if you can experience in your history something of what I have experienced in the knowledge of the Lord’. Most here will know that when I say that if ministry does anything it sends us to the Lord for ourselves, I am just quoting Mr. Raven. It cannot do anything else; it takes you to the Lord for yourself so that you have your history and your knowledge, and you develop in fibre and strength in your knowledge of God, so that you are standing on your own feet with God and not leaning on props. Even if they are good props, eventually they will be taken away, and what then? Thank God for father and mother and their influence, thank God for the environment into which they have introduced you. Thank God for the brothers in the meeting that help you the most, and thank God for the brothers that give the lead in the meeting, those that pray for you; but to give efficacy to all that it needs to be made good in your own soul and in your own personal links with God, otherwise eventually you will fall away.

Now the Lord would encourage us about this and I selected Jacob because he had a very chequered history. He started as a young man. He went out from his father’s house and did many things that in these days we would think quite wrong; but what was before him was God, and God’s purpose. We should have said about Jacob, Well, he twisted his brother out of what belonged to him; he was a cheater and a twister. I do not know what you think, but Esau would be a far more attractive man to me than Jacob. Out in the field, well, I like that, with bows and arrows, hunting, and so on; much better than the homely man who sits there making carpets and things like that; I do not think much of that.

Esau, speaking naturally, is a much more attractive man; but he had not before him the purpose of God. Jacob had, and, despite his chequered history, as he went through he was developing in his knowledge of God. That is what I would like you to do. He was developing in his knowledge of God as an individual. He spent a lot of time alone, you know. When he set up that pillar as a pillow, you remember, he was alone. He had a wonderful vision of the angels of God ascending and descending on the ladder. He learned that God was interested in him.

I would like to tell you young people that God is interested in you, anxious, if I can apply such a word to God, that you should know Him and grow in the knowledge of Him, and day by day in your experiences learn Him in them. You may be just starting school; it may be you are just starting business; it may be some other turn in life, just starting married life maybe; in all these things God wants you to grow in the knowledge of Himself, and I will tell you this—in any of these turns in life, the knowledge of God, and bringing God into those circumstances, will never weaken your enjoyment of them, but it will rather strengthen your confidence in Him and strengthen your enjoyment of what He has given you, without those things turning you away from Himself. I think Jacob learned that as he went on.
Well, here we find him in Genesis 32 and he is going to meet his brother and for him that was not a very pleasant anticipation. He was going to meet his brother who had vowed to kill him.

Well, that was not a very pleasant outlook was it? but he takes it up with God. It says he was left alone. Have you ever been alone with God? I am sure there are many here who have been alone with God. It says, “And Jacob remained alone”. I would love to be more alone with God. I have not much capacity to sustain the presence of God; I would love to develop in it, and it develops with practice. Men say, and there is a lot in it, you know, that practice makes perfect. You practise prayer, practise meditation, practise reading the Scriptures, practise approaching God. If you feel your weakness and the enemy’s power, persevere. One often says you never tell a child to persevere in something he finds easy, you tell him to persevere in a lesson he finds difficult; so persevere.

I think Jacob here is an example of a man who is persevering with God. It says, “and a man wrestled with him”; no doubt that was God. I will not touch too much on the fact that the other man took the initiative; what I would desire to emphasize is that Jacob held on; he persevered in this wrestling; “I will not let thee go except thou bless me”. He persevered. We must take things up individually with God. Of course, the time comes when we pray for others, but here he is persevering in prayer in regard of his own blessing, and the man says to him, “What is thy name? And he said, Jacob. And he said, Thy name shall not henceforth be called Jacob”. He gets a spiritual name. Have you a spiritual name? I think God would have us be conscious of a spiritual name in the sense that the Spirit gives you a distinctive impression of Christ. This has often been likened to Romans 7 and 8, so that when he comes out of the experience the sun was shining on him—“there is then now no condemnation to those in Christ Jesus”, no condemnation; not merely that they are not condemned, but such a thing as condemnation just does not exist, so that they could not be condemned today and not tomorrow, or not today and then tomorrow; it just does not exist. The sun was shining; that is what Jacob comes to, and he gets a spiritual name, Israel, “for thou hast wrestled with God, and with men, and hast prevailed”.

You know, dear brethren, it is a great thing to persevere in prayer until you are conscious that God is listening to you; not that He is going to say ‘yes’ necessarily, but you are conscious that He is listening to you. Oh, you say, He hears everything, the faintest, feeblest cry. You know that objectively, but I think it is a great thing to be conscious that God is listening to you in your exercises, not only in relation to your own personal matters but also in relation to His matters, His testimony, His rights, His glory in our several localities. Well, Jacob had to come to that; this is a step in that direction; but the flesh was crippled. There is no doubt about it, there is nothing like the presence of God to cripple the flesh in its activities. So it says, “he limped upon his hip”. He would have limped for the rest of his life, ever conscious of that experience, but ever conscious that every step from that day forward would be a step in dependence upon God. Now we all have to learn that, so that we have no confidence in the flesh. We “worship by the Spirit of God, and boast in Christ Jesus, and do not trust in flesh”, Philippians 3: 3. So you can think of Jacob throughout his life of 147 years, a long time after this, and in every step in every day he would be conscious that

God had affected him, that the flesh was crippled, and that he must henceforth walk in simple dependence upon God. What history the man had! I could refer to the latter part of his life in which he speaks of the God who had shepherded him all his life long till that day, so though he has to say “few and evil have been the days of the years of my life”, he speaks also of the God that had shepherded him and he desires that that God should bless the lads, the sons of Joseph (see Genesis 48: 15, 16).
Now I speak of Peter, another man who had what we call a somewhat chequered history.

Those of us who are getting a little older have been very thankful for these men. I am sure they would never have objected to our learning from their experiences. It has often been said that it is a wise man who learns from his experience, and it is a wiser man who learns from other people’s too. So we can learn from the experience of Jacob and Peter. Here we find the disciples in the ship and it says “the ship was already in the middle of the sea tossed by the waves, for the wind was contrary”. Do we not find in our localities that the wind is contrary?

Satan attacks what is precious to Christ always. I do not think he is much interested in that which is not precious to Christ, but he attacks and seeks to unsettle—if I might use the simple illustration—the local ‘boat’ where there are those who are devoted to Christ. What the measure of their devotion is we will leave, but they are devoted to Christ; and these disciples were, and Satan tries to unsettle the boat. I think it makes history in their souls in their knowledge of the Lord. I think in particular it makes history in Peter’s soul, so that this became a landmark in his history. But as Jacob was with the Lord so is Peter. It has been recorded for you and me. What history am I making? You say, we have difficulties in our locality; well we all

have difficulties and exercises in our localities. Mr. Jethro Jay once said to me, ‘You show me the meeting without exercise and I will very quickly show you the meeting without any life’. If you have life in your meeting you will have exercises; you will have the boat, so to speak, rocking at times. It is all to test the moral fibre of the occupants of the boat, I think. It is what God does in our localities so that He tests us and His work in us. He tests our confidence in Himself and in the Lord.
Well, Peter says to the Lord, “If it be thou, command me to come to thee upon the waters”.

Jesus just says, “Come”. “But seeing the wind strong he was afraid; and beginning to sink he cried out, saying, Lord, save me”. I think one simple lesson from this is one that has often been referred to, that you keep your eye on Christ. I remind you of that; to me it is not irksome to say that you must keep your eye on Christ, not on the wind that is strong, or on the waves, which are the enemy’s tactics; do not be over-occupied with what he is doing although, of course, we are not ignorant of his thoughts. Keep your eye on Christ and what He is doing; see what the Lord is doing. He told them to go in the boat; He told them to go to the other side, and you can be sure that if He tells you to go to the other side you will get there. I have every confidence at this moment that the Lord will see His testimony through.

The only doubt that exists as far as I am concerned is whether I shall be in it or not. I would be exercised to be in it until He comes, but I am persuaded He will see it through. I think that would be one lesson that Peter would have learned from this incident in his soul history, that he should keep his eye on the Lord, who is really the Master of the ship. Peter was not that.
The wind fell and the Lord showed

that He was in supreme command. I think Mr. McBride once said that it would be time enough for him to be afraid when the Man on the throne was afraid. When will that be? Well, never! The Man on the throne is not disturbed; time enough for me to be disturbed when the Man on the throne is disturbed! He is in complete control and He shows it, but, dear brethren, although we say that, and know it as an objective truth, we have to learn it, personally and in our localities, experimentally. So, as another has said, ‘all is lost to those who say all is lost’.

Now this dear woman in Matthew 26 also had soul history with God. I think the alabaster flask of very precious ointment which she poured out on His head as He lay at table would be the result of her history with God. It may have been in very mundane circumstances. I do not know what she did day by day. It may be she was learning God in the household chores, as we say. It must be very testing to sisters day after day to be at the sink washing up and doing the washing and the housework. But if you bring God into it, if you refer each matter to God, however mundane it may be, I think you will gain some of this precious ointment. It will bring a savour into the meeting. I believe that our dear sisters give substance and character to our occasions; I am sure of it. You often find if you go to a meeting where there are a number of elderly and devoted sisters that the way is made easy because of their influence, their link with the Lord, their appreciation of Him, what they have learned in those long years of work, mundane work, day after day. It may have been very boring, but they have learned the Lord in it; they have learned to love Him; they do things as serving the Lord Christ however simple they may be (see Colossians 3: 23, 24). In it they are growing in the knowledge of God.

Can you take things up like that? I find it difficult, I admit. You get up and go to work; you come home and go to the meeting, and then go home and go to bed, and so on; it all seems very mundane and routine. If you can seek grace to bring God into it I think you grow in the knowledge of Him because He enters into the details of our lives far more than we think. He has in mind all the time our development in the knowledge of Himself; and, after all, that is the most precious possession we have, the knowledge of God. May the Lord encourage us all to be exercised to grow in that knowledge and to develop in it by growing in soul history, personal history, day by day with Himself. May it be so for His name’s sake.
Lord Jesus, mighty Son of God,
Thou glorious Heir of all,
We own Thee now supreme in love
And thus before Thee fall;
Greater than all, ascended high,
Eternally the Same,
Yet speaks of grace and lowliness
Thine ever-precious Name.
‘Tis Thou, O Lord, who didst descend,
Didst make Thyself as nought,
Wearied, alone, despised, disowned,
Forsaken and unsought;
But now we celebrate Thy love,
Thou who for us didst die,
Yet Thou art He, the Same, unchanged,
For e’er gone up on high.
Who shall, O Lord, ascend above?
O’er every heaven Thou!
All things Thou’rt great enough to fill;
All shall before Thee bow!
But now to sing Thy praise we join
—All praises Thou above—
Till heav’ns and earth in glad response
Bring answer to Thy love.
Kingston, Ont.

“CHRIST LIVES IN ME” Everything for the believer is established “in Christ” and “in Christ Jesus”; then there is another rich line of thought relating to what Paul speaks of as “the riches of the glory of this mystery among the nations, which is Christ in you the hope of glory”—

Christ in you. It is Christ enshrined in the mind and the affections; He dwells there. In Galatians 2: 20 Paul says, “I am crucified with Christ, and no longer live, I, but Christ lives in me”. That is a very active thought, lives in me. It implies that the power of Christ’s life is operating in the believer. Clearly, if Christ thus takes up His abode all must be subject to Him. He must be in supreme control, all the reins of our life must now be in His hand. This must have powerful and manifest results. If Christ is dwelling in the seat of our affections, thoughts, and motives, then He will be expressed in our spirits and actions. What a fine thing that is, that the character and ugliness of the old ‘ I’ are no longer in evidence; instead the precious features of Christ are shining out. Mr. Darby described it as ‘The living display of what Christ is before men’, adding, ‘We should never be content when we fail to display Christ before men’ (‘Coll. Wrtgs.’, Vol. 12, p392).
May we be greatly exercised that the reality of this may increasingly work out in us.

What is divine is never lost; it may be covered with the plaster of this world, but whatever has been written on the fleshy tables of the heart will never be effaced. You will certainly sing again as in the days of your youth, but then you must be brought to the valley of Achor.

Achor is sorrow; it is morally the death of all that which turned away the heart from God, and this can take place without actual bereavement here. It is renunciation in sorrow. It is a condemning to death the natural attractions which stole the heart away from the bright line in which God has set it; and this is known by the consciousness the heart has of returning to where it had left off. Like one long absent from a loved home returning to it, or the hound returning to the lost scent, which delights and commands all the energies of his existence.

There is a sense of renewed connection with the light once enjoyed and the path once trodden; and there is the self-condemnation and repudiation of the imaginary pleasures which had diverted one from it. There must be in some way a discovering of the worthlessness of everything, to set one in the path of life with God.
